intro: Each year council adopts a financial plan that sets how much money the District of Squamish raises from property taxes. In 2026, the money raised from property taxes went up 12.8%. For the average single family home, the municipal part of the tax bill rose about $520.

Staff's draft for 2027, presented on September 29, 2026, starts at a 10.4% increase, or about $342 for the average home. Most of that, 6.6%, is costs already committed, such as wage contracts, police contract costs, transit and debt payments for new facilities. Another 2.4% goes to a reserve for repairing and replacing roads, pipes and buildings. Items still waiting for council approval would add more.

For comparison, prices in British Columbia were 3.0% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier. Staff costs and contracts for a town do not always move with consumer prices. The new council takes over the draft. Adoption is expected in early 2027 (last year it was adopted January 13). These numbers are a draft as of October 2026 and will change.

facts.label: 2027 starting draft
facts.value: 10.4%, about $342 for the average home, before new items

facts.label: Already committed
facts.value: 6.6% of the 10.4% (wages, police, transit, debt and more)

facts.label: Infrastructure reserve
facts.value: 2.4% of the 10.4%, under the District's asset funding plan

facts.label: Forecast for 2028
facts.value: 12.7% increase, before items still to be approved

timeline.what: Council adopted the District's first 10 year financial plan.
Staff presented the draft 2027 general fund budget with a 10.4% starting increase.
Council budget workshop to tie the plan together.
Public information night (date to be confirmed) and adoption of the financial plan bylaw.

points: After a 12.8% jump in 2026, many households need a break, and a freeze forces a hard look at every cost.
It would mean cutting or delaying services, repairs or projects, since most of the starting increase is costs already committed.
Keeps tax growth in line with what households are seeing in prices, about 3% in B.C. this year.
Council would need to find savings or delay new spending to close the gap with the 10.4% draft.
Squamish is growing fast and has aging roads, pipes and buildings; putting off repairs can cost more later.
Staff say most of the starting increase comes from contracts, debt and reserve payments that are hard to avoid.

questions.q: Does a 10.4% increase mean my bill goes up 10.4%?
questions.a: Not exactly. It is the increase in total tax revenue. Your share depends on how your assessment changed compared with others.

questions.q: How can I give my view?
questions.a: Email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca, use the questions on the Let's Talk Squamish budget page, or attend the budget information night.
6.6% for committed costs, 2.4% for the infrastructure reserve, 1.3% for service changes already endorsed or critical, and 0.1% for critical special projects.
